ranke.label: Critical historical scholarship
ranke.date_label: Earlier philological roots · Ranke’s preface 1824 · later archival scholarship
ranke.description: Source criticism and historical particularity develop through many traditions: philology, antiquarian research, ecclesiastical scholarship, archives, and university seminars. Ranke is a major exemplar, not their sole origin. Its approaches distinguish documentary authenticity, language and meaning, historical questions, and interpretation of conditions; these operations can support political, social and cultural subjects.
ranke.representative_figures_and_works: Leopold von Ranke (1795–1886); archival practice spreads far beyond political and diplomatic subjects. This tradition is not simply synonymous with positivism.

representative_people.context: Combines close documentary work with relations among events, peoples and epochs. Historical individuality and religious commitments coexist; his selected European scope and civilizational judgments are contestable, and he is not the sole origin of criticism.
representative_people.works: History of the Popes (1834–1836; Austin translation 1840); 1824 historical preface; lectures on epochs (1854); selected World History reflections

representative_people.context: Salmon explicitly recalls his teaching on judging an author by the purpose of a work. Placement in this broad critical-scholarship entry does not establish Ranke transmission.

ranke.scope_note: Ranke is an exemplar within older critical practices. Archival scholarship is neither exclusively political nor simply positivist. Mabillon, Droysen and the French methodologists expose different practices and disagreements. Ranke’s theological and exclusionary claims are not atlas assumptions; critical inquiry has non-European histories beyond this selected European genealogy.

strands.title: Document authenticity and archival authority
strands.focus: Material/textual comparison and the authority claimed for sovereign archives provide different grounds of documentary proof. Older practices have their own controversies; no single line of descent is assumed.
strands.works: De re diplomatica (1681); Propylaeum antiquarium (1675), through Head’s scholarly abstract

strands.title: Close sources and historical relations
strands.focus: Ranke’s strict factual ambition coexists with synthesis, political/religious interdependence and ideas. The research program is not merely accumulation of facts.

strands.title: Epochs, progress and theological judgments
strands.focus: Ranke resists a uniform ladder of moral or artistic improvement and values periods in themselves. His theological grounding and civilizational exclusions qualify any universal reading.

strands.title: Criticism, conditions and interpretation
strands.focus: Droysen treats authentication as preparation for interpretation, acknowledges gaps and the historical value of falsification, and limits access to personality while examining wider conditions.
strands.works: Outline of the Principles of History (1893), selected §§20–41

strands.title: Historical language and the meaning of a source
strands.focus: Meaning varies with usage, time, author and surrounding text. Establishing what a source says differs from deciding whether its claims are true; hidden allusions remain conjectural.
strands.works: Introduction to the Study of History, II.6

strands.title: Teaching, manuals and critical disagreement
strands.focus: Methodological instruction and published manuals supply resources through explicit acknowledgment, criticism and adaptation. Bernheim’s and Fustel’s reception differs from Tyler’s instruction recalled by Salmon.
strands.works: Langlois/Seignobos preface; Salmon, Progress in the Household (1906), Apologia

strands.title: Critiques of documentary sufficiency
strands.focus: Croce questions abstract source categories; Lamprecht contests explanatory priorities. Their different objections do not establish that authentic documents are useless or that all critical scholars share one doctrine.

nationaltradition.label: National & imperial narratives
nationaltradition.description: National and imperial histories join source work to competing accounts of peoples, states, liberty and civilization. Michelet, Macaulay and Bancroft differ in method and purpose; colonial hierarchies, liberation histories and critiques of nationalist exclusions remain in tension.
nationaltradition.representative_figures_and_works: A broad context of historical production, not one school: nation-building, colonial institutions, and resistance generate different and often conflicting projects.

representative_people.context: Interweaves archives, geography, cultural life and a self-forming French people. The 1869 preface admires and disputes Thierry, credits Vico and reflects on the historian’s participation. His revolutionary history later becomes Barthes’s narrative example.
representative_people.works: Histoire de France (1833–1867), preface of 1869; Histoire de la Révolution française (1847–1853); later analysis in Barthes (1968)

representative_people.context: Connects constitutional settlement, commerce, empire and everyday manners while acknowledging crimes and failures. His education minute argues for a hierarchy of knowledge and English-trained imperial intermediaries. Distinct from Catharine Macaulay.
representative_people.works: The History of England from the Accession of James II, volume I, chapter I; “Minute on Indian Education” (2 February 1835)

representative_people.context: Combines comparative documentary criticism with a story of liberty developing from colonial institutions. His professed impartiality does not establish equal representation of all inhabitants.
representative_people.works: History of the United States / History of the Colonization of the United States, volume I (first-edition preface 1834; consulted 17th edition 1859)

representative_people.context: Uses Michelet and Thierry to question narrative transparency and examine how writing signifies historical reality. These readings do not dismiss all national histories or independently refute their factual claims.
representative_people.works: “The Discourse of History” (1967); “The Reality Effect” (1968)

representative_people.context: Michelet admires his national narrative while criticizing an explanatory commitment to the permanence of races; this is an attributed reception, not a reading of Thierry’s original work.

anticolonial.description: Recasts empire through slavery, resistance, liberation, and colonized peoples’ historical agency. modern.label: Modernization theory
modern.description: Explains change through transitions from traditional to modern societies. Often takes Western development as the model; social-scientific variants differ. Growth stages, democratic legitimacy and political institutionalization answer different questions. Eisenstadt’s later multiple-modernities program disputes convergence on one Western pattern while retaining comparative inquiry.
modern.representative_figures_and_works: W. W. Rostow, The Stages of Economic Growth (1960); Daniel Lerner, The Passing of Traditional Society (1958); Talcott Parsons, “Evolutionary Universals in Society” (1964); Seymour Martin Lipset, “Some Social Requisites of Democracy” (1959).

representative_people.context: Proposes five growth stages with qualified timing and some change within the traditional category. His dynamic-production discussion combines sectoral change and political choices; the staged hierarchy remains contestable.
representative_people.works: The Stages of Economic Growth (1960), chapter 2, pp. 4–16

representative_people.context: Communication researcher linking media, changing dispositions, and modernization; his Cold War model is historically situated.
representative_people.works: The Passing of Traditional Society (1958)

representative_people.context: Compares institutional arrangements through proposed evolutionary universals and adaptive capacity. Explicitly uses Durkheim and Weber while acknowledging variation; his hierarchical and political predictions remain authorial claims.

representative_people.context: Tests proposed associations among development, legitimacy and democracy. He distinguishes legitimacy from effectiveness and explicitly rejects guaranteed democratization, noting provisional comparisons and multivariate causes.
representative_people.works: Some Social Requisites of Democracy (1959), selected pp. 69–71, 84–87, 102–104

representative_people.context: Uses action theory and differentiation to frame changes in British cotton production and family life. The checked description identifies the project; Thompson’s separate primary criticism should not replace reading Smelser.

representative_people.context: Distinguishes political institutionalization from growth or electoral form and argues that mobilization can outpace institutional capacity. His priority of order and regional generalizations are situated, contested claims.

representative_people.works: “The Paradigmatic Crisis in Chinese Studies” (1991); “Further Thoughts on Eighteenth-Century Britain and China” (2003)

modern.scope_note: Economic stages, communication and social dispositions, institutional differentiation, and democratization are distinct explanations. These contributors are not all historians, and the models do not form one inevitable path. Lipset explicitly denies automatic democratization, Huntington prioritizes institutional capacity, and Eisenstadt’s 2000 argument revises convergence assumptions. These differences do not erase hierarchical categories, Cold War purposes or disputed empirical claims in earlier models; a later program is not projected into every 1950s text.

strands.title: Economic stages
strands.focus: Rostow proposes five growth stages, qualified timing and a dynamic production theory attentive to sectors and policy choices. Permitting variation does not establish the staged hierarchy as a universal history.
strands.works: The Stages of Economic Growth (1960), chapter 2, pp. 4–16

strands.title: Communication and social dispositions
strands.focus: Mass media and changing orientations within a Cold War account of modernization.

strands.title: Social differentiation and institutions
strands.focus: Parsons proposes adaptive institutional universals with variable historical development; Smelser applies differentiation/action theory to cotton industry and family change. Their specific claims and Thompson’s criticism must be distinguished.

strands.title: Development and democratic legitimacy
strands.focus: Lipset separates economic development, legitimacy and effectiveness, investigates probabilistic associations and explicitly denies that greater prosperity guarantees democracy. His comparative coding and statistics remain open to testing.
strands.works: Some Social Requisites of Democracy (1959), selected pages

strands.title: Political institutionalization and order
strands.focus: Huntington asks whether organizations and procedures acquire stability and value as social mobilization increases. Adaptability, complexity, autonomy and coherence are proposed criteria; order-first priorities and empirical comparisons remain contestable.
strands.works: Political Order in Changing Societies (1968), pp. 1–7, 12–13

strands.title: Individual change and measured dispositions
strands.focus: Inkeles and Smith’s project distinguishes individual orientations and their possible settings from national growth stages. Available contents identify a scale and comparative research design; those headings alone do not establish its validity or causal findings.

strands.title: Multiple modernities and contested cultural programs
strands.focus: Eisenstadt’s 2000 account separates modernity from Westernization and recognizes changing programs within and across societies. It includes destructive forces and challenges to the nation-state, without making every difference a timeless civilizational essence.

strands.title: Comparative methods, translations and collaboration
strands.focus: Lipset specifies Schumpeter/Weber definitions and Lazarsfeld’s multivariate resource; Parsons cites Durkheim/Weber and acknowledges seminar discussion with Bellah/Eisenstadt. Shared resources do not erase distinct explanatory aims.

social.label: New social history
social.description: An overlapping field of work, class formation, households, community and collective action. Thompson, Davis and Gutman already integrate culture and agency; demographic and mobility studies use distinct evidence. Davidoff and Hall connect gender and middle-class life; Chakrabarty and Cooper investigate colonial labor and the limits of inherited categories. Scott’s critique makes experience itself a historical question, not something to discard.
social.representative_figures_and_works: E. P. Thompson and Eric Hobsbawm; Herbert Gutman, Work, Culture, and Society in Industrializing America (1976); Natalie Zemon Davis, Society and Culture in Early Modern France (1975); Charles Tilly; E. A. Wrigley and historical demography. Earlier social inquiry provides comparisons, not membership in a later school. Further readings: Davidoff and Hall, Family Fortunes (1987); Chakrabarty, Rethinking Working-Class History (1989); Scott, “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); Cooper, Decolonization and African Society (1996). Geoff Eley and Keith Nield: “Why does social history ignore politics?” (1980).

strands.title: Politics within social-history debate
strands.focus: Eley and Nield asked in 1980 why social history ignored politics (article unread; they recalled in 2007 that it 'drew disappointingly little response in print' and that they had been 'trying to create a space for political analysis in the expanded sense given to "politics" by the politics of knowledge of 1968', 2000, p. 14). Joyce's 'The End of Social History?' (1995; unread) drew their 'Starting Over' (1995; unread), which Joyce said equated his questioning of social history 'with contemporary neo-liberalism' (1996). In 'Farewell to the Working Class?' (2000, read in full) they held that 'class discursively understood … is a better starting point' while wanting 'to break this logic of disavowal' (p. 16); Scott's reply (read in full) called this 'Assent to Discourse' and objected that insisting on class forecloses other political categories (p. 69); Cooper answered that 'they did not think to ask Karl Marx' (p. 61). The debate entry languages_of_class holds the exchanges.
strands.works: “Why does social history ignore politics?” (1980), coauthored; “Starting Over” (1995); “Farewell to the Working Class?” and reply (ILWCH 57, 2000); The Future of Class in History (2007)

strands.title: Genealogy, values and historical explanation
strands.focus: Nietzsche’s critique asks both how moral judgments arise and what they are worth; Rée and Schopenhauer are distinct interlocutors. Origin and later function must not be conflated.

strands.title: Rhetoric, reference and historical achievement
strands.focus: Barthes analyzes the presentation of reality; Bann uses that analysis while questioning its scope and preserving source-based scrutiny. Formal analysis alone does not decide a historical claim’s truth.

strands.title: The historian, surviving sources and the historical picture
strands.focus: Michelet’s account of reciprocal formation and Huizinga’s warning about surviving art raise different questions about historical knowledge; they do not deny the need for evidence.

strands.title: Evidence, understanding and the historical question
strands.focus: Droysen, Dilthey, Croce and Collingwood offer different accounts of what inquiry does with traces, thought, context and practical concerns. These are explicit conceptual resources, not a common doctrine or a proved genealogy of later debate.

strands.title: Language use and following rules
strands.focus: Wittgenstein examines varied activities and similarities rather than one essence of language. Following a rule involves a practice; an interpretation cannot supply its own application without limit.

strands.title: Knowing how, action and accomplishment
strands.focus: Ryle distinguishes competent action from both an automatic movement and a performance governed by an endless series of prior theoretical decisions. A richer action description identifies purpose and circumstances.
strands.works: The Concept of Mind, II.1–3; The Thinking of Thoughts

strands.title: Narrative and historical understanding
strands.focus: White identifies particular philosophical interlocutors rather than responding to one undifferentiated philosophy of history.

strands.title: Laws, probability and explanation sketches

strands.title: Action and the limits of one explanatory model
strands.focus: Dray’s challenge includes reasons, uniqueness and pragmatic questions; it is not a ban on all generalization.
strands.works: Laws and Explanation (1957); Nature of Historical Explanation (1952)

strands.title: Selection, relevance and revisable interpretation

historicalsociology.label: Comparative historical sociology
historicalsociology.description: Compares how states, rights, class relations and collective struggles change. Moore studies agrarian routes; Skocpol combines state breakdown with class and international relations; Tilly follows contention; Mann maps intersecting power networks. Bendix, Goldstone, Somers and Block supply different questions about authority, demography, citizenship and economic institutions. Sewell’s exchange with Skocpol makes ideology an explicit debate.

africanhist.label: African history: postwar institutional expansion
africanhist.date_label: Older traditions · Ibadan · Dar es Salaam · expansion from the 1950s
africanhist.description: Postwar institutions challenge colonial denials of African historical agency while building on older African historical knowledge and writing. Nationalist, Marxist, social, and cultural projects overlap and contend; their institutional expansion is not the beginning of African historical thought.

intellectualhistory.label: Intellectual history
intellectualhistory.date_label: Earlier histories of thought · Lovejoy 1936 · Skinner 1969 · plural programmes through the 1990s
intellectualhistory.description: Studies thought, concepts, arguments and their production, circulation and interpretation in historical settings. History of ideas, contextual political thought, conceptual history, textual criticism and the material history of publishing supply overlapping but disputed methods. Intellectual history extends beyond the Cambridge School and beyond a canon of European philosophers.

intellectualhistory.scope_note: An enduring field with internal disagreements, not a single lineage from Lovejoy to contextualism. The existing Cambridge School and Conceptual history entries retain their specificity. Maruyama supplies one Japanese inquiry with explicit translation credit, not global representation or evidence of Cambridge influence. Social and cultural settings matter without reducing texts to reflections of social position. Women’s intellectual histories and African, Islamic, South Asian and Latin American traditions still need much fuller coverage.
